title: Why Almost Nobody Lives on Namibia's Skeleton Coast

paragraphs.text: Namibia's Skeleton Coast and the desert shore south of it run for more than thirteen hundred kilometres along the Atlantic. That is about as long as the whole coast of California.

shots.on_screen_text: Where the Namib meets the Atlantic

paragraphs.text: But almost nobody lives on it. We counted where Namibians live, and only about one in fourteen lives within fifty kilometres of the sea.

shots.on_screen_text: The dune sea meets the Atlantic

stat.label: Of Namibians live within 50 km of the sea
stat.source: Own count: Kontur population 2023 (CC BY 4.0) vs the coastline (geo/measure_population.py)

shots.on_screen_text: The empty coast south of Walvis Bay

paragraphs.text: So why does almost nobody live on Namibia's Skeleton Coast?
The answer runs through a harbour that belonged to another country until 1994, a rescue that wrecked a tug and a bomber, and a diamond town that was closed to outsiders until 2017.

shots.on_screen_text: A wreck on the Skeleton Coast

paragraphs.text: The first reason is the sea itself.

chapters.title: A Sea That Will Not Rain

paragraphs.text: Reason one. The ocean off this coast is cold, and cold water does not make rain.

A current called the Benguela carries water up from the south, and winds lift colder water from the deep to the surface. The air above it is chilled from below. It stays low and heavy, and the clouds that would bring rain never build.

shots.on_screen_text: Cold upwelled water along the shore

paragraphs.text: Walvis Bay, the biggest town on the coast, gets about half an inch of rain a year. Windhoek, the capital, up on the plateau, gets more than twenty times as much.
What the sea does give is fog. On many mornings it rolls inland, and the beetles and plants of the Namib live on the drops it leaves. People cannot.

shots.on_screen_text: The dunes inland of the coast

paragraphs.text: Behind the beach lies the Namib, a desert of gravel plains and some of the tallest dunes on earth. In many places they run straight into the sea.

shots.on_screen_text: Sandwich Harbour: dunes into the sea

paragraphs.text: South of Walvis Bay the sand sea is about three hundred and twenty kilometres long. Its northern edge is a dry river, the Kuiseb, and the dunes stop at its bed as if at a wall.

shots.on_screen_text: The Kuiseb: dunes stop at the riverbed

paragraphs.text: Rivers cross it rarely. Most of them reach the coast only after heavy rain far inland, and some years not at all.

shots.on_screen_text: The Kuiseb nearing the sea, from the ISS
The Kunene, the only river that always flows

paragraphs.text: A coast with no rain, no rivers and no farmland gave people no reason to stop. And the first Europeans who saw it did not stop either.
Reason two. Ships need water and a safe harbour, and this coast had almost neither.
In January 1486, the Portuguese captain Diogo Cão landed at a headland north of today's Swakopmund and set up a stone cross to claim it. Then he sailed on.

stat.label: Diogo Cão's stone cross at Cape Cross

paragraphs.text: The headland is still called Cape Cross. Today it belongs to seals. In the breeding season up to two hundred and ten thousand Cape fur seals crowd its rocks, the largest colony of its kind in the world.

shots.on_screen_text: The seal colony at Cape Cross

stat.label: Seals at Cape Cross in the breeding season

paragraphs.text: That cross stood there for four hundred years. In 1893 a German naval officer took it to Berlin, where it stood in a museum for more than a century. Namibia asked for it back in 2017, and in 2019 it was shipped home.

stat.label: The cross is shipped back to Namibia

paragraphs.text: For four centuries after Cão, sailors mostly passed by. There was nothing on the shore to stop for.

shots.on_screen_text: The coast north of Cape Cross

paragraphs.text: Along the whole coast there was one good natural harbour: Walvis Bay, a deep bay sheltered by a sandspit.

shots.on_screen_text: Pelican Point, the sandspit that shelters Walvis Bay

paragraphs.text: Britain claimed it in 1878, and in 1884 made it part of its Cape Colony. That same year, Germany claimed the land all around it.

stat.label: Britain claims Walvis Bay; Cape Colony from 1884

paragraphs.text: Germany's claim began with a merchant from Bremen, Adolf Lüderitz. In May 1883 he bought a sheltered cove in the south, Angra Pequena, and five miles of land around it from a Nama chief, Josef Frederiks, for a hundred pounds in gold and two hundred rifles.

shots.photo: File:Lüderitz Territory (formerly Angra Pequena), today Lüderitz, Namibia German Medal 1884, obverse.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: German medal for the Lüderitz territory, 1884

stat.label: Price of Angra Pequena, May 1883

paragraphs.text: A second contract that August took a strip of land to the Orange River, measured in miles. The chief understood English miles. The contract meant German geographical miles, almost five times longer. It became known as the mile swindle.

stat.label: A German geographical mile against an English mile

paragraphs.text: Lüderitz went to look for minerals on the Orange River in 1886 and never came back. The cove was renamed after him: Lüderitz.

shots.photo: File:ISS-62 Orange River, Namibia and South Africa.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Orange River from the ISS

paragraphs.text: So the Germans had a colony with a coast, but the only good harbour on that coast was British.
They tried to make one of their own at Swakopmund, thirty kilometres to the north. In 1903 they opened a stone pier, the Mole, to shelter the landing boats.

shots.photo: File:Molo ve městě Swakopmund - Namibie - panoramio.jpg

paragraphs.text: Within about two years the sea had filled it with sand. Ships had to unload into small boats again, and later onto a wooden jetty.

shots.photo: File:Molo ve městě Swakopmund - Namibie - panoramio (2).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Mole, long since filled with sand

shots.photo: File:Molo ve městě Swakopmund - Namibie - panoramio (3).jpg

paragraphs.text: They had already built a railway, to carry everything from the poor landing at Swakopmund up to the capital. The line to Windhoek, three hundred and eighty-two kilometres of narrow track, opened in June 1902.

stat.label: Swakopmund-Windhoek railway, opened June 1902

paragraphs.text: Swakopmund grew as a German town at the end of that line, and today it is Namibia's seaside resort. But its sea front was never a real harbour.

shots.photo: File:Mission Church and building - Rheinische Missionsgesellschaft - Swakopmund - 1938.jpg

paragraphs.text: The bay stayed in other hands for a long time. When the British Cape became part of South Africa in 1910, Walvis Bay went with it.

stat.label: Walvis Bay passes to the Union of South Africa

paragraphs.text: Namibia became independent in 1990. Walvis Bay did not. Its only deep-water port stayed South African for four more years, until the first of March 1994.

stat.label: Walvis Bay handed over to Namibia

paragraphs.text: So for a century, the one place where a coastal city could grow was the one place the country running the coast did not own. And the rest of the coast was busy sinking ships.
Reason three. The coast is dangerous to reach even from the sea.

shots.on_screen_text: A wreck on the Skeleton Coast

paragraphs.text: Fog hides the shore, the surf is heavy, and sandbanks shift. Over the centuries hundreds of ships ran aground here. Their rusting hulls, with the bones of whales and seals on the beaches, gave the Skeleton Coast its name.

shots.on_screen_text: The Eduard Bohlen, now inland in the dunes

paragraphs.text: The story that shows it best began on the twenty-ninth of November 1942.

stat.label: The Dunedin Star strikes a shoal

paragraphs.text: The British cargo ship Dunedin Star, carrying 106 people, struck a shoal off the northern coast. Her captain ran her onto the beach to save her.

shots.on_screen_text: The coast where the Dunedin Star was beached

paragraphs.text: Many of the passengers and crew got ashore through the surf. The beach was dry, cold at night and hundreds of kilometres from any town.

shots.on_screen_text: Hundreds of kilometres from any town

paragraphs.text: A rescue began from three sides. A tug, the Sir Charles Elliott, came up from Walvis Bay. It too ran aground on the coast, and two of its crew drowned.

stat.label: Crew of the tug Sir Charles Elliott who drowned

paragraphs.text: The air force sent a Ventura bomber to drop supplies. It landed on the beach to help, and its wheels sank into the sand, and it could not take off again.

stat.label: South African Air Force bomber sent to help

shots.on_screen_text: The beach near the wreck site
Soft sand on the Skeleton Coast

paragraphs.text: Its pilot, Captain Naude, and his three crew were now stranded too. The rescuers needed rescuing.

stat.label: The Ventura's crew, now stranded too

paragraphs.text: In the end, a police convoy of trucks under Captain Smith crossed the desert from Windhoek to fetch the people ashore. They reached Windhoek on Christmas Eve, almost four weeks after the wreck.

shots.on_screen_text: The desert between the coast and the interior

stat.label: Survivors and airmen reach Windhoek

paragraphs.text: Every one of the ship's passengers survived. But the coast had taken a ship, a tug and a bomber in a single month. That is the coast people were trying to live on.

shots.on_screen_text: A wreck on the Skeleton Coast

stat.label: Lost in one month, Nov-Dec 1942

paragraphs.text: Most of that northern coast is now the Skeleton Coast National Park, proclaimed in 1971. Its southern half can be driven with a permit. The northern half can only be reached by small plane, with one licensed tour company.

stat.label: Skeleton Coast Park proclaimed

shots.on_screen_text: The roadless north of the park

paragraphs.text: Even the park's fishing camps open only for the season. Torra Bay takes campers in December and January, and is closed the rest of the year.
And on the southern coast, it was not the sea that kept people out. It was a law.

shots.on_screen_text: Henties Bay, the last town before the park

paragraphs.text: Lüderitz carries a darker memory too. During the war against the Herero and Nama, from 1904 to 1908, the German army held prisoners on Shark Island in Lüderitz bay. Between September 1906 and March 1907, more than a thousand of its seventeen hundred prisoners died.

shots.photo: File:Lüderitz - Saint Peter and Saint Paul Catholic Church.jpg

stat.label: Prisoners who died on Shark Island, Sep 1906 - Mar 1907

paragraphs.text: In 2021 Germany said that the killings were, from today's perspective, a genocide, and asked Namibia for forgiveness. The talks about what that means are still going on.

stat.label: Germany: genocide 'from today's perspective'

paragraphs.text: Reason four. In the south, the most valuable land on the coast was closed to almost everyone.

shots.photo: File:Wild desert between Oranjemond and Rosh Pinah South Namibia (1).jpg

paragraphs.text: In April 1908, a railway worker named Zacharias Lewala was clearing sand from the line near Lüderitz when he picked up a shiny stone. It was a diamond.

stat.label: Zacharias Lewala finds a diamond

paragraphs.text: The desert floor was scattered with them. Within months the colonial government closed off a huge strip of the coast, about twenty-six thousand square kilometres. It was called the Sperrgebiet, the forbidden area.

stat.label: The Sperrgebiet, the forbidden area, 1908

paragraphs.text: Inside it, the mining companies built towns for their own workers. At Kolmanskop there was a hospital for up to two hundred patients, an ice factory and a ballroom, in the middle of the dunes. The hospital is said to have had one of the first X-ray machines in the southern hemisphere, and some accounts say it was used to look for stolen diamonds.
When richer deposits were found further south, the workers moved on. By 1956 Kolmanskop was empty, left to the sand, which now fills its rooms to the windowsills.

stat.label: Kolmanskop abandoned

paragraphs.text: The new centre was Oranjemund, at the mouth of the Orange River. It was a company town. For decades nobody could go there without a permit from the mining company.

shots.on_screen_text: The Orange River mouth and Oranjemund

shots.photo: File:Wild desert between Oranjemond and Rosh Pinah South Namibia (1).jpg

paragraphs.text: Namibia made it a town in 2011, but it was only opened to the public on the twenty-first of October 2017.

stat.label: Oranjemund opens to the public

paragraphs.text: Today the diamonds are mined by Namdeb, owned half by the state and half by De Beers. Most of the old forbidden area is now a national park, Tsau Khaeb.

shots.photo: File:ISS-62 Orange River, Namibia and South Africa.jpg

paragraphs.text: The closed zone even kept a treasure safe. In 2008, mining near Oranjemund uncovered the wreck of the Bom Jesus, a Portuguese ship lost in 1533. It held more than two thousand gold and silver coins.

stat.label: Gold and silver coins of the Bom Jesus (lost 1533)

paragraphs.text: Under the sand the diggers found about seventeen tonnes of copper ingots and more than a hundred elephant tusks as well. Portugal gave up its claim, and the treasure stayed in Namibia.

stat.label: Copper ingots from the Bom Jesus

paragraphs.text: Diamonds made the southern coast rich, and they kept it nearly empty. So where do the people of the coast actually live?
Reason five. The few who do live here are packed into two towns, and those towns run on water they make and rock they dig.

We wanted to know how many Namibians really live near this coast. So we took a population map of the whole country, made from satellite images and the census, and measured each small square's distance from the sea.

About seven per cent of Namibians live within fifty kilometres of the Atlantic. Go a hundred kilometres inland and the share barely moves. Beyond the towns, almost nobody lives anywhere near this coast.

chart.title: Namibians living near the sea
chart.source: Own count: Kontur population 2023 (CC BY 4.0) vs the coastline (geo/measure_population.py)

shots.on_screen_text: The empty coast south of Walvis Bay

paragraphs.text: We measured how far the coastline runs without a single settled square. South of Walvis Bay, almost five hundred kilometres of coast pass with nobody living by the sea.

stat.label: Of coast without a settled square
stat.source: Own count: Kontur population 2023 (CC BY 4.0) vs the coastline (geo/measure_population.py)

paragraphs.text: North of the old diamond coast, the same is true for more than three hundred kilometres, up to the Angolan border.

stat.label: Of empty coast up to the Kunene
stat.source: Own count: Kontur population 2023 (CC BY 4.0) vs the coastline (geo/measure_population.py)

paragraphs.text: Walvis Bay has about a hundred thousand people, and Swakopmund about seventy-six thousand. Together they hold most of the people on the whole coast.

shots.on_screen_text: Walvis Bay's port from the air

paragraphs.text: And they are growing fast. The region around them grew by almost sixty per cent between 2011 and 2023.

stat.label: Growth of the Erongo region, 2011-2023

paragraphs.text: One reason is the port: Walvis Bay is Namibia's door to the world, for fishing boats, ships and trucks to the interior.

In 2019 a new container terminal opened there, built on about forty hectares of land reclaimed from the bay. It more than doubled the port's capacity, to about seven hundred and fifty thousand containers a year.

shots.on_screen_text: The 2019 container terminal on reclaimed land

stat.label: Container capacity a year after 2019

paragraphs.text: The cold, rich sea also feeds one of Africa's big fisheries. Fishing gives about sixteen thousand direct jobs, most of them in the fish plants of Walvis Bay and Lüderitz, and hake alone gives more than ten thousand.

stat.label: Direct jobs in fishing

paragraphs.text: The other is uranium. Inland from Swakopmund lie some of the largest uranium mines in the world. Rössing has been digging since 1976, and in 2024 Namibia produced about an eighth of the world's uranium.

stat.label: Namibia's share of world uranium, 2024

paragraphs.text: The towns drink from under a dry river. Walvis Bay's water is pumped from the sands of the Kuiseb, through a pipeline built in the 1970s, and the town has no other source. A 2021 report by the water company, cited by The Namibian, found the town using more than the aquifer can sustainably give.

shots.on_screen_text: The Kuiseb, where Walvis Bay's water comes from

stat.label: Walvis Bay's only water source: the Kuiseb aquifer

paragraphs.text: Mines and towns need water, and there is almost none. So in 2010 a plant was built on the coast to turn seawater into fresh water. It was the first large plant of its kind in sub-Saharan Africa.

stat.label: First large seawater desalination plant in sub-Saharan Africa

shots.on_screen_text: Henties Bay, north of the plant

paragraphs.text: In 2025 it produced about seventeen and a half million cubic metres of water, and most of it went to the mines.

stat.label: Water from the Erongo desalination plant, 2025

paragraphs.text: The plant was built for up to forty-five million cubic metres a year, and the uranium miners want a second one. The towns, meanwhile, are short of homes. Walvis Bay counts a backlog of about thirty-five thousand houses, and Swakopmund about thirty-two thousand.

stat.label: Housing backlog in Walvis Bay

paragraphs.text: So people can live on this coast. But only where a port, a mine and a plant that makes water all come together.
Reason six. The empty coast is valuable precisely because it is empty, and now someone wants to fill part of it.

Near Lüderitz, a company called Hyphen plans to make green hydrogen with sun and wind. The project covers about four thousand square kilometres inside the national park and would cost around ten billion dollars.

stat.label: Hyphen's green hydrogen project

paragraphs.text: Namibia's government has taken a stake of about a quarter. The decision on whether to build is due by the end of 2026.

stat.label: Namibian state stake in the project

paragraphs.text: Lüderitz badly needs work, and many of its people want the project. Conservationists warn about penguins and seabirds on the islands nearby and about building inside a park.

shots.on_screen_text: African penguins at Halifax Island, off Lüderitz

paragraphs.text: And offshore there is another bet. In 2022 Shell and TotalEnergies found oil deep under the sea off the southern coast. Analysts expect the first oil around the end of this decade, and a gas pipeline is planned to come ashore near Lüderitz.

stat.label: Oil found offshore in the Orange Basin

paragraphs.text: If those projects go ahead, the empty south could fill with workers again, a century after the diamond rush.

The empty coast has users of its own. In the national park, two prides of desert lions have learned to hunt on the beach, taking seals, flamingos and cormorants. They are the only lions known to live on prey from the sea.

shots.on_screen_text: The Hoanib mouth, where the lions hunt

paragraphs.text: The ministry counts only about a hundred desert lions in the whole northwest. Every road and pipe on this coast passes through their range.

stat.label: Desert lions in northwest Namibia

paragraphs.text: It is the same question the coast has always asked. Is it worth bringing people, water and power to a place that never wanted them?
So this is why almost nobody lives on Namibia's Skeleton Coast.

The cold sea gives fog instead of rain. The one good harbour belonged to someone else until 1994. Ships, tugs and even a bomber were lost on the shore. Diamonds closed the south for a century. And the towns that did grow live on a port, uranium and water made from the sea.
About one Namibian in fourteen lives near this coast. Almost all of them live in two towns, with hundreds of kilometres of empty beach on either side.
Every attempt to settle this shore has needed something rare: a deep bay, a diamond, a mine, or a machine that makes water. Where those were missing, the coast stayed empty, and it still is.
Should Namibia open its empty coast to new industry, or keep it the way the desert made it?

ask.text: Open the empty coast to industry, or keep it as the desert made it?

youtube.description: Namibia's Atlantic coast runs for more than 1,300 km, yet only about one Namibian in fourteen lives within 50 km of the sea. We follow why: the cold Benguela sea that brings fog instead of rain, the one good harbour at Walvis Bay that stayed British and South African until 1994, Swakopmund's harbour that filled with sand, the Dunedin Star rescue of 1942 that cost a tug and a bomber, the diamond Sperrgebiet and the ghost town of Kolmanskop, Oranjemund closed until 2017, the uranium mines and the seawater plant that keep the coast towns alive, and the green hydrogen and oil bets on the empty south.
